title: Receptive fields: where, and how precisely
objective: Explain receptive fields and why skin is mapped precisely while internal organs are not.

steps.title: Each neuron 'owns' a patch
steps.body:
A neuron's **[[receptive field]]** is the region where a stimulus can change its firing. On the fingertip, touch receptive fields are tiny and densely packed. On the back, they are large and sparse.

Small fields plus high density means fine spatial detail. That's why you can read Braille with a fingertip but not with your back.

steps.setup: In a two-point test, you touch the skin with two points and ask whether the person feels one or two.
steps.prompt: Where will two points need to be farthest apart to feel like two?
options: Fingertip
Lips
Middle of the back
Tongue tip
steps.reveal: The back has large, sparse receptive fields, so two points close together land in the same field and feel like one. Fingertips, lips and tongue have the smallest fields.

variants.prompt: Two-point discrimination is finest (smallest distance still felt as two) where receptive fields are…
options: Large and widely spaced
Small and densely packed
Absent altogether
All exactly the same size
variants.explanation: Fine spatial resolution comes from small, dense receptive fields (fingertip, lips, tongue); large sparse fields (the back) blur two points into one.

variants.prompt: Where are two-point touch receptive fields largest and most sparse?
options: The pad of the fingertip
The middle of the back
The surface of the lips
The very tip of the tongue
variants.explanation: Large, sparse fields (the back) merge two nearby points into one; fingertips, lips and tongue have tiny dense fields and fine spatial resolution.

steps.title: Organs are mapped coarsely
steps.body:
Internal organs get far fewer sensory fibers than skin. Each visceral afferent typically covers a large territory, and their signals [[converge]] in the cord with input from the skin (D3, D5).

The result is poor localization: gut sensations feel vague and spread out, and are sometimes referred to the body wall.

flag.note: Visceral receptive fields vary by organ and afferent type; the point is the contrast with skin.

steps.prompt: Why can't you point to exactly where in your colon a cramp is?
options: The colon has essentially no sensory neurons of its own to report with
Visceral afferents are sparse, with large fields that converge with skin input
Colon pain travels only by the vagus, which carries no spatial information
Colon afferents fire too fast for the cord to resolve their position
steps.explanation: Sparse innervation, large receptive fields and convergence together blur location. That makes visceral pain hard to localize and prone to referral.

variants.setup: A patient reports a cramp 'somewhere in my belly' but can't point to where.
options: The colon has essentially no sensory neurons of its own to report with
Visceral afferents are sparse, with large fields that converge with skin input
Colon pain travels only by the vagus, which carries no spatial information
Colon afferents fire too fast for the cord to resolve their position
variants.reveal: Few afferents, large receptive fields, and convergence onto shared spinal levels make visceral pain poorly localized and prone to referral.

steps.prompt: You want to map the receptive field of a single colon-innervating DRG neuron. What do you need to vary?
options: Vary only the stimulus intensity while holding the probe in one spot
Move a small punctate stimulus across the colon wall while recording the cell
Vary the mouse's age across a cohort and average the responses together
Vary the fluorophore color used to label that neuron's ending
steps.explanation: A receptive field is defined by location: you move a small probe around and note where the neuron responds. This is how single-afferent ending territories are characterized.

variants.prompt: To find a single colon afferent's receptive field, the key thing to vary is…
options: How bright the labeling dye on the fiber is
Where on the colon wall a small probe is applied
The age of the mouse you are recording from
How long each individual recording session lasts
variants.explanation: A receptive field is defined by location: move a punctate stimulus around and note where the cell responds.

reviewNotes: Textbook-level. 'converge' links to new glossary term convergence.
